hero.eyebrow: Free and open source for Linux
hero.title: A fast, native download manager for Linux.
hero.desc: Bengal Download Manager splits files into parallel connections, catches downloads from your browser, and resumes interrupted transfers automatically. It is a lightweight Qt application — no Electron, no ads, no telemetry.

features.title: Parallel downloads
features.text: Files are split into up to 32 chunks and transferred at once, making better use of the available bandwidth.

features.title: Browser integration
features.text: The Chrome and Firefox extensions catch download links and hand them to the app over a secure local port.

features.title: Pause and resume
features.text: Transfers resume from the last byte when a connection drops, so large files do not start over.

features.title: Media downloads
features.text: Paste a video or audio URL to read its metadata, preview a thumbnail, and choose a resolution or bitrate.

features.title: Automatic categories
features.text: Incoming files are sorted into Documents, Videos, Music, Compressed, and Programs folders by type.

features.title: Native desktop interface
features.text: Follows your system light and dark theme, with support for both Wayland and X11 sessions.

faq.title: Common questions
faq.desc: A short overview of how the app works and what it supports.

items.q: Why is Bengal Download Manager faster than browser downloads?
items.a: Browsers download files through a single continuous TCP stream, which is often throttled by servers or slowed by packet loss. Bengal Download Manager breaks the file into up to 32 parallel chunks (powered by Aria2) and transfers them at the same time.

items.q: Is it a good IDM alternative on Linux?
items.a: Yes. Internet Download Manager is Windows-only and not available natively on Linux. Bengal Download Manager is built for Linux and provides multi-segment acceleration, one-click browser interception, automatic category sorting, and reliable pause and resume support.

items.q: What makes it different from other download managers?
items.a: It pairs the Aria2 download engine with a native PyQt6 interface instead of an Electron shell. It starts quickly, uses little memory, follows your desktop theme, and ships without ads, bundled software, or telemetry.

items.q: How does the browser extension capture links?
items.a: The Chrome and Firefox extensions watch for download triggers using Manifest V3 APIs. When a matching file type is detected, the download is handed to the app through a local loopback connection on port 56800.

items.q: Can I pause and resume interrupted downloads?
items.a: Yes. Pause and resume works with any server that supports HTTP byte ranges. If the connection drops or the computer sleeps, the transfer continues from the last completed byte.

It runs on major distributions including Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora, Arch Linux, openSUSE, Linux Mint, Manjaro, and Pop!_OS. Packages are available through Flathub, Snap, a direct Flatpak repository, and portable AppImage builds for x86_64 and aarch64.

items.q: Is it completely free and open source?
items.a: Yes. Bengal Download Manager is released under the MIT License. There are no subscriptions, no ads, no bundled software, and no telemetry. You can audit, contribute to, or fork the code on GitHub.
